candidates.topic: Lobsters Are Biologically Immortal — They Don't Age
candidates.teaser: One ocean creature technically never gets old — and science can prove it.
candidates.video_title: Lobsters Don't Age. Here's Why That's Terrifying.
candidates.video_description: Lobsters possess an enzyme that prevents cellular aging — they don't weaken with age, they grow stronger. The only reason they die is external. This challenges everything we think we know about biological mortality.
candidates.script: A lobster doesn't age. Not slowly — not at all. They carry an enzyme called telomerase that repairs their DNA every single time a cell divides, something human cells stop doing around age 25. An older lobster is actually stronger, faster, and more fertile than a young one. The only reason they ever die is being eaten, disease, or the sheer exhaustion of molting their own shell. Left alone, a lobster could theoretically live forever. So why can't we?

candidates.topic: The Sedlec Ossuary — Church Built From 40,000 Human Bones
candidates.teaser: There's a church in Europe where every decoration — every single one — is made of human bones.
candidates.video_title: A Church Decorated Entirely With 40,000 Human Bones
candidates.video_description: The Sedlec Ossuary in the Czech Republic contains the skeletal remains of 40,000 people, arranged into chandeliers, coats of arms, and wall decorations. It was completed in 1870 and remains an active place of worship today.
candidates.script: In a small Czech town, there's a church where the chandelier hanging above you is made entirely of every bone in the human body — not a single one missing. The Sedlec Ossuary holds the remains of roughly 40,000 people, victims of plague and war, arranged into decorations by a half-blind monk in 1511. Skulls line the walls. Femurs form archways. A noble family's coat of arms — made of bones — hangs near the altar. And every year, tourists line up to pray inside it.

candidates.topic: The Carrington Event — Solar Storm That Nearly Ended Civilization
candidates.teaser: In 1859, a solar storm hit Earth so hard that telegraph wires burst into flames — and if it happened today, we'd have no warning.
candidates.video_title: The Solar Storm That Nearly Burned the World in 1859
candidates.video_description: The 1859 Carrington Event was the most powerful geomagnetic storm ever recorded. Telegraph systems worldwide failed, caught fire, and still operated without power. Scientists estimate a repeat event today would cause up to $2 trillion in damage and knock out global power grids for years.
candidates.script: In September 1859, telegraph operators across America and Europe were electrocuted at their desks. The machines kept sending messages even after being unplugged. The night sky glowed so bright that miners in the Rocky Mountains woke up thinking it was morning. A solar storm had just struck Earth with the force of ten billion atomic bombs. Scientists call it the Carrington Event. If the same storm hit today, it would collapse every power grid on the planet — and we'd have roughly 17 minutes of warning.

candidates.topic: Hiroo Onoda — Japanese Soldier Who Fought for 29 Years After WWII Ended
candidates.teaser: One soldier kept fighting World War II until 1974 — because nobody could convince him it was over.
candidates.video_title: The Soldier Who Refused to Believe WWII Was Over for 29 Years
candidates.video_description: Hiroo Onoda, a Japanese intelligence officer, continued guerrilla warfare in the Philippine jungle until 1974 — nearly three decades after Japan surrendered in 1945. He only laid down his weapon when his former commanding officer flew in personally to relieve him of duty.
candidates.script: In 1974, a Japanese soldier emerged from a Philippine jungle, rifle in hand, still fighting World War II. Hiroo Onoda had been waging a guerrilla campaign for 29 years — since 1945. He'd found leaflets saying Japan surrendered. He assumed they were enemy propaganda. Search parties, newspapers, even his own family couldn't reach him. The war only ended for him when his original commanding officer — now 77 years old — flew to the jungle and personally ordered him to stop.

candidates.topic: The Uncanny Valley — Why Almost-Human Faces Feel Horrifying
candidates.teaser: There's a precise point where a human face becomes so realistic that your brain decides it's a corpse — and scientists have measured exactly where it is.
candidates.video_title: Why Almost-Human Faces Terrify Your Brain
candidates.video_description: The uncanny valley is a measurable psychological phenomenon where near-perfect human replicas — robots, CGI faces, hyper-realistic dolls — trigger deep feelings of dread and revulsion. Neuroscientists believe it's an ancient survival mechanism designed to detect disease, death, or deception.
candidates.script: Your brain has a threshold. Up to a certain point, the more human something looks, the more you like it. Cross that line by just a fraction — a robot's face too smooth, a CGI character's eyes slightly too still — and your brain doesn't just feel uncomfortable. It fires the exact same signals it uses to detect a corpse. Scientists call it the uncanny valley. It's not a metaphor. It's a measurable dip in your emotional response. Your mind is literally screaming: something here is pretending to be alive.
